entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, known as Tarquin the Proud, was the legendary seventh and final king of Rome, reigning for approximately 25 years from 535 BCE to 509 BCE. His reign marks the definitive end of the Roman monarchy and directly precipitated the establishment of the Roman Republic. A figure of immense historical consequence, his story is foundational to Roman identity, encapsulating the city's transition from an Etruscan-influenced kingdom to a self-governing republic. His rule was characterized by tyranny and military expansion, ultimately leading to a popular uprising spearheaded by figures like Lucius Junius Brutus, deeply embedding an anti-monarchical sentiment in Roman political thought for centuries.

Tarquin ascended to the throne through violence, orchestrating the assassination of his predecessor and father-in-law, Servius Tullius, with the complicity of his wife, Tullia Minor. He consolidated power by executing or exiling senators and ruling without consulting the Senate or the people, disregarding traditional Roman law. Despite his tyrannical methods, Tarquin was a significant builder, initiating major public works such as the completion of the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitoline Hill and the construction of the Circus Maximus's first permanent seating. He also pursued aggressive military campaigns, conquering Gabii and establishing Roman dominance over the Latin League.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Lucius Tarquinius Superbus's tyrannical reign and ultimate expulsion marked the definitive end of the Roman monarchy and the birth of the Roman Republic in 509 BCE, fundamentally altering the trajectory of Roman and subsequently Western political development for centuries. His story became a foundational narrative for Roman identity, embodying their deep-seated aversion to kingship.
